findings.title: `summary!` lies for every unsummarised book — Chat and Quiz crash on any Goodreads-imported title
findings.description: `BookDetailProps.summary` is honestly typed `Summary | undefined` (line 119), and the component correctly optional-chains it everywhere it renders text (lines 452, 461, 470, 490) and guards it in both async handlers (`if (!summary) return;` at 158 and 183). Then lines 534 and 536 assert it away with `!` to satisfy `ChatModalProps.summary: Summary` and `QuizModalProps.summary: Summary`. The invariant that would make those assertions true does not exist: the Chat and Quiz buttons at lines 340 and 347 are gated only on `!isPreview`, never on `summary`. BookDetailPage.tsx:40-53 never passes `isPreview`, so on the real route both buttons always render. A book with no summary is a first-class state in this app — useLibrary.tsx:150-160 (`importGoodreadsRows`) deliberately creates books with no `summaryId` and no summary record so that Goodreads import stays free, and useBookRoute.ts:12 additionally starts every book at `summary === undefined` until an async IndexedDB read resolves. Clicking Chat then runs ChatModal.tsx:37 -> createBookChatSession(book, undefined) -> chatSystemInstruction(book, undefined) -> prompts.ts:61 `${summary.oneSentenceTakeaway}` -> TypeError, thrown from inside a useEffect with no try/catch, which unmounts the whole route into the react-router errorElement. Clicking Quiz runs QuizModal.tsx:43 -> generateBookQuiz -> quizPrompt -> prompts.ts:48 `${summary.summary}` -> the same TypeError, but there it is swallowed by quiz.ts:18's `catch { throw toAiError(error) }` and normalised to kind 'unknown', so the user is told 'Something went wrong talking to Gemini. Try again.' for what is actually a null dereference in our own code. The two `!` are the only reason the compiler does not already reject this.
findings.suggestedPatch: Delete both `!` and let the compiler enforce the invariant, by narrowing at the render site instead of asserting: change lines 534/536 to `{showChat && summary && <ChatModal ... summary={summary} ... />}` and `{showQuiz && summary && <QuizModal ... summary={summary} ... />}`. That alone stops the crash. Pair it with the UX half so the buttons cannot lie either: at lines 339-348 add `disabled={!summary}` (plus a `title`/`aria-label` explaining 'Generate a summary first') to both buttons, or render the pair only when `summary` is present. No signature change is needed anywhere else — ChatModalProps and QuizModalProps stay `summary: Summary`, which is the correct contract; the fix is to stop lying to it.

findings.title: importLibrary declares payload: LibraryExport for a hand-editable JSON file that is never validated; a single `{}` entry persists a Book with title undefined and crashes the library route permanently
findings.description: `importLibrary(payload: LibraryExport)` declares that `payload.books` is `Book[]` and `payload.summaries` is `Summary[]`, both required and fully populated. The runtime value is `JSON.parse(fileContents) as LibraryExport` (ProfileView.tsx:117, itself fed by `e.target?.result as string`) — an arbitrary user-supplied file. The author knew the type lies: lines 109 and 114 write `payload.books ?? []` and `payload.summaries ?? []`, defensive code that is provably dead under the declared type. The only real guard is `Array.isArray(data.books)` at ProfileView.tsx:119; nothing checks the ELEMENTS, and nothing checks `summaries` at all. Exact input: `{"version":2,"exportedAt":"x","books":[{}],"summaries":[]}` — any JSON with a `books` array of non-Book objects, e.g. another app's export. It passes the guard; `bookRepo.create({...book, profileId})` fills in only `id` and `addedAt`, so a record with `title: undefined` is written to IndexedDB (verified in node). Broken consumer: LibraryPage.tsx:50 runs `book.title.toLowerCase()` inside the filter, throwing `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined` (verified) before a single card renders. Because the corrupt record is PERSISTED, the library route crashes to the error boundary on every subsequent load; the book cannot be opened to delete it, and the only escape is Danger Zone -> Reset All, which destroys the whole library. Second consumer: `libraryToMarkdown` -> `bookToMarkdown` (markdown.ts:24) dereferences `summary.keyInsights.length` on unvalidated imported summaries, and ProfileView.tsx:320 calls `void handleExportMarkdown()` with no catch, so Markdown export silently does nothing.
findings.suggestedPatch: Change the parameter to `payload: unknown` and add a narrowing guard in useLibrary.tsx that returns 0 (or throws a typed ImportError) unless the payload matches: a small `isBook(value): value is Book` / `isSummary(value): value is Summary` pair checking the required string fields, applied with `.filter(isBook)` at line 109 and `.filter(isSummary)` at line 114. Delete the now-redundant `Array.isArray` check at ProfileView.tsx:119 and report the skipped-record count to the user. Risk: users importing older/hand-edited backups will see records silently dropped rather than half-imported, so the toast copy at ProfileView.tsx:133 should report the skip count.

findings.title: createBookChatSession is typed as total but throws MissingKeyError; its only consumer calls it bare inside useEffect, so the no-key path replaces the whole app with the error boundary
findings.description: `createBookChatSession(book, summary): Chat` declares that it always yields a Chat. It cannot: `getClient()` (src/lib/ai/client.ts:11) throws `MissingKeyError` whenever `localStorage` holds no Gemini key, and the catch block re-throws it as an AiError. This is the ONLY synchronous AI entry point in the codebase — every other one (`summarizeBook`, `generateBookQuiz`, `generateAudioSummary`, `sendMessageStream`) is `async`, so its throw becomes a rejection that the caller's try/catch absorbs. Here the throw is synchronous and the sole consumer, ChatModal.tsx:36-38, invokes it inside a `useEffect` with no try/catch. Exact input: a user with no API key (the default for every fresh install) opens any book and clicks the 'Chat' button (BookDetail.tsx:340 sets showChat with no key gate). Broken consumer: the throw escapes the effect, react-router's route `errorElement` (routes.tsx:16) catches it, and the ENTIRE app — nav, library, everything — is replaced by 'Something went wrong'. This directly violates the documented project invariant 'The app works with no key... Only AI actions gate, and they open the key dialog': instead of opening ApiKeyDialog, the app bricks itself. No test covers this path.
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the contract honest at the source: change the signature to `createBookChatSession(book, summary): Chat | null`, returning null when `getApiKey()` is absent (or keep the throw and change the return to a `{ ok: true; chat: Chat } | { ok: false; error: AiError }` result). Then in ChatModal.tsx:36-38 wrap the effect body in try/catch and route the failure through `useShell().handleAiError`, which already opens the key dialog — the same handling every other AI action gets. Risk: ChatModal must gain a 'no session' render branch, so the fix touches its render as well as its effect.

findings.title: migrateLegacyData declares Promise<MigrationResult> but rejects on malformed legacy data; ProfileContext awaits it with no catch, so the app hangs on the loading spinner forever and re-duplicates data on every retry
findings.description: `migrateLegacyData(): Promise<MigrationResult>` claims it always resolves to a result object. It has at least four reachable rejection paths, all over data the app does not control: (a) `readJson<T>(key): T | null` (line 54-62) is a bare `JSON.parse(raw) as T` with zero shape validation, so if `booksum_library_<id>` holds a JSON object instead of an array, `for (const legacy of legacyBooks)` at line 101 throws `TypeError: ... is not iterable` (verified in node); (b) `base64ToBytes(legacy.pdfData)` at line 136 throws `DOMException: Invalid character` on any malformed base64 (verified in node) — and legacy records are exactly the multi-megabyte base64 PDFs that CLAUDE.md says 'broke the original app', so truncated/quota-clipped values are likely; (c) the same at line 142 for `audioData`; (d) `blobs.put` / `books.create` reject with QuotaExceededError when those same PDFs are re-written into IndexedDB. Broken consumer: ProfileContext.tsx:30-42 runs `void (async () => { await migrateLegacyData(); ... setIsLoading(false); })()` with no `.catch`. A rejection skips `setIsLoading(false)` entirely, so `App.tsx:12` renders the full-screen spinner forever — and `main.tsx` has no top-level error boundary, so nothing else fires either. Worse, `localStorage.setItem(MIGRATION_MARKER, ...)` on line 149 is only reached on success, so every reload re-runs the migration from scratch: `profiles.create()` mints a NEW uuid each time, leaving a duplicate profile plus a partial book set per attempt. Silent data duplication behind a permanent spinner.
findings.suggestedPatch: Two-part fix. (1) Make the failure mode representable: add `failed: number` (or an `errors: string[]`) to `MigrationResult` and wrap the per-book body (lines 101-146) in try/catch so one bad legacy record is counted and skipped instead of aborting the run; move the MIGRATION_MARKER write so it lands even on a partially-failed run, which is what actually prevents duplication. (2) At the consumer, ProfileContext.tsx:31, wrap in try/catch (or `.catch`) and always `setIsLoading(false)` in a finally so the app boots even when migration fails. Also narrow `readJson<T>` to return `unknown` and add an `Array.isArray` check at line 99. Risk: changing MigrationResult's shape touches migrate.test.ts assertions.

findings.title: The boot path treats the erased localStorage->IndexedDB migration as infallible; one throw wedges the app forever
findings.description: F007 covers the cast (`JSON.parse(raw) as T` at migrate.ts:58). This is its blast radius, in a file no lot covered. ProfileProvider's mount effect awaits `migrateLegacyData()` inside a `void (async () => ...)()` with no try/catch, and `setIsLoading(false)` is the last statement. If the migration rejects, `isLoading` stays `true` forever, `App.tsx:12` renders the spinner, no router ever mounts, and there is no in-app recovery — the user must manually clear site data. Reachable throws all originate at the erased boundary: `readJson<LegacyBook[]>` returns whatever was under `booksum_library_*`, and if that is an object rather than an array, `for (const legacy of legacyBooks)` at migrate.ts:101 throws TypeError (verified: 'is not iterable'); `base64ToBytes(legacy.pdfData)` calls `atob`, which throws DOMException on non-base64 (verified); and an IndexedDB quota or blocked error rejects too. The migration is also completely untested against malformed input — all 8 cases in migrate.test.ts seed well-formed JSON.
findings.suggestedPatch: Two-part. (1) In migrate.ts, make readJson honest: change the signature to `readJson(key: string): unknown` and have callers narrow — `const list = readJson(k); const legacyBooks = Array.isArray(list) ? list : [];` and `const p = readJson(k); const legacyProfile = p && typeof p === 'object' ? (p as LegacyProfile) : null;`. Also wrap each base64ToBytes call in a try/catch that skips that one blob instead of aborting the whole migration. (2) In ProfileContext.tsx wrap lines 31-41 in try/catch/finally so `setIsLoading(false)` runs in the `finally`, and surface the failure with `toast.error` — a legacy import that partly fails must still let the app boot. Risk: none to behaviour on the happy path; a previously-fatal migration now completes partially, so log what was skipped.

findings.title: QuizQuestion[] is asserted straight off the model with no bounds check; `options: string[]` implies non-empty and `correctAnswerIndex: number` implies in-range, and the unvalidated values are persisted as ReviewCards that permanently jam the review queue
findings.description: `generateBookQuiz(...): Promise<QuizQuestion[]>` mints `QuizQuestion` values from `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { questions?: QuizQuestion[] }`. `QuizQuestion.options: string[]` (types.ts:107) carries an implicit non-empty promise and `correctAnswerIndex: number` an implicit in-bounds promise; the Gemini responseSchema (schemas.ts:64-72) only says ARRAY-of-STRING and NUMBER — no minItems, no range — and a grep of the whole repo confirms NOT ONE site checks `options.length` or bounds-checks `correctAnswerIndex`. The values do not stay in memory: QuizModal.tsx:52-60 copies each question verbatim into `newCard(...)` and writes it to IndexedDB as a `ReviewCard`, which repeats the same two lies at types.ts:88-89. Exact input: the model returns `{"questions":[{"question":"Q","options":[],"correctAnswerIndex":0,"explanation":"E"}]}`. Broken consumer: ReviewPage.tsx:93 renders `current.options.map(...)` -> zero buttons, so `selected` never leaves null, so `isAnswered` is false, so the grade buttons at line 125 never render — and `grade()` (useReviewQueue.ts:33-41) is the ONLY thing that removes a card from the queue. That card sits at `queue[0]` forever: the review feature is permanently unusable for that profile with no in-app remedy. The sibling lie is quieter and more likely: a 1-based `correctAnswerIndex` (a classic model slip) makes every answer score as wrong forever, in both QuizModal.tsx:78 and ReviewPage.tsx:76, with no error anywhere.

findings.title: @google/genai types `responseSchema` as `Schema | unknown`, so all three response schemas are completely unchecked
findings.description: This is an implicit-any escape hatch of exactly the `import.meta.env` shape, and it governs the contract for every AI response the app parses. node_modules/@google/genai/dist/genai.d.ts:12090 declares `export declare type SchemaUnion = Schema | unknown;`. A union with `unknown` collapses to `unknown`, so `GenerateContentConfig.responseSchema?: SchemaUnion` (genai.d.ts:5204) accepts literally any value. The three schema objects in this file — GENERIC_BOOK_SCHEMA (line 3), RECOMMENDATION_SCHEMA (line 36), QUIZ_SCHEMA (line 55) — carry no type annotation, so nothing ever checks them against the SDK's real `Schema` type. `strict: true` and `noImplicitAny` are both on and neither helps. PROVEN: a probe compiled against the repo's real @google/genai under strict mode passes `{ typ: Type.OBJECT, propertes: { title: { type: 'STRNIG' } }, requiredd: ['title'], totallyMadeUpField: 12345 }` as `responseSchema` with zero errors, and `responseSchema: 42` also compiles. Blast radius: these schemas are the only thing constraining what Gemini returns for summarize.ts (two call sites), quiz.ts and recommend.ts, and each of those then does `JSON.parse(response.text) as <hand-written interface>`. The schema and the interface it is supposed to mirror (RawBookResponse at line 87) are two independent hand-maintained descriptions of the same shape with no compiler link between them — rename a property in one and nothing anywhere fails. A silent typo in a key name degrades the model's structured output rather than erroring, which surfaces as an empty summary, not a stack trace.
findings.suggestedPatch: Isolate the SDK's looseness at the one place it enters by annotating the three exported constants with the SDK's own type — `import { Type, type Schema } from '@google/genai';` then `export const GENERIC_BOOK_SCHEMA: Schema = {...}`, `export const RECOMMENDATION_SCHEMA: Schema = {...}`, `export const QUIZ_SCHEMA: Schema = {...}`. This is verified zero-risk: a probe annotating the repo's current schema literals with `Schema` compiles clean, so no existing schema changes shape and no runtime behaviour moves. The annotation restores excess-property checking (misspelled keys become errors) and enum checking on every `type:` field. schemas.ts is already the correct single shim file for this — nothing else in the repo constructs a Schema — so the whole vendor hole closes with three type annotations.

findings.title: The DBSchema declaration is the single assertion that makes all ten IndexedDB reads look type-safe
findings.description: Every prior repo.ts finding is a symptom of this one declaration. `BookSumDB extends DBSchema` tells `idb` that the `profiles`/`books`/`summaries`/`blobs`/`reviewCards` stores contain Profile/Book/Summary/StoredBlob/ReviewCard, and `idb` propagates that as the return type of get/getAll/getFromIndex/getAllFromIndex with zero runtime cost and zero runtime checking. There is no validation anywhere in src/lib/storage, so what comes out is whatever was put in. The lie is realisable and self-inflicted, not hypothetical: `useLibrary.importLibrary` (F022) writes objects straight out of an unvalidated backup file into `books` and `summaries`, and `migrateLegacyData` writes objects derived from unvalidated localStorage. Once a malformed record lands, every subsequent read in every future session returns it typed as a valid domain object, and the corruption survives reloads permanently. Per the audit spec's type-assertion-cluster guidance, the fix belongs at the SOURCE — this declaration — not at the ten consumers.
findings.suggestedPatch: Re-type the source rather than the consumers. Change the schema's `value` types to a raw shape (`value: unknown`, or `value: Partial<Book> & { id: string }`) and add one hand-written narrowing guard per entity in a new `src/lib/storage/guards.ts` — `isBook(v: unknown): v is Book` etc., checked with `typeof`/`Array.isArray`. Then make repo.ts the only place that applies them: `getAll` results go through `.filter(isBook)` and `get` results through `isBook(r) ? r : undefined`. That keeps the repo's public signatures identical (`Promise<Book[]>`, `Promise<Book | undefined>`), so no caller changes, and it closes F004/F022's blast radius at the read side as well as the write side. Risk: filtering silently drops corrupt records, so log a count and surface it once via toast rather than dropping in silence.

findings.title: getDb memoizes the promise before it settles and never clears it on rejection, so one transient IndexedDB open failure permanently poisons every Promise<T> in the repo for the rest of the session
findings.description: `getDb(): Promise<IDBPDatabase<BookSumDB>>` is the root of every storage contract in the app, and its declared type says nothing about failure. `dbPromise` is assigned synchronously at line 23 and is only ever cleared by the test-only `resetDb()`. If `openDB` rejects even once — storage denied in Safari private browsing, a blocked upgrade because another tab holds the old version, the user clearing site data mid-session, or an origin over quota — the REJECTED promise stays cached, and every later `getDb()` returns that same rejected promise. There is no retry path. Every declared-total signature downstream then lies at once: `profiles.list(): Promise<Profile[]>`, `books.listByProfile(): Promise<Book[]>`, `summaries.getByBook(): Promise<Summary | undefined>`, `blobs.get(): Promise<Blob | undefined>` — all reject. Broken consumers, none of which catch: `useLibrary.reload` (useLibrary.tsx:22-34) never reaches `setIsLoading(false)`, so the library shows its spinner forever; `ProfileContext` (ProfileContext.tsx:30-42) likewise never clears `isLoading`, so App.tsx:12 renders the full-screen spinner and, with no top-level error boundary in main.tsx, nothing is ever reported to the user. This is a distinct root cause from RT-F002 with the same terminal symptom.
findings.suggestedPatch: Clear the memo on failure so the next call retries: `dbPromise = openDB(...).catch((error) => { dbPromise = null; throw error; })`. That keeps the declared `Promise<IDBPDatabase<BookSumDB>>` honest for the retry case; separately, add a `.catch` in useLibrary.tsx:37 and ProfileContext.tsx:30 that sets `isLoading` false and raises a toast, so a hard storage failure shows a message instead of an eternal spinner. Risk: retrying an open that fails deterministically (private browsing) will re-attempt on every repo call — bound it with a one-shot 'storage unavailable' flag if that proves noisy.

findings.title: `routeTable` is an exported value with no `RouteObject[]` annotation, so route-key typos compile silently
findings.description: `routeTable` is exported (and consumed by src/app/routing.test.tsx as well as by AppRoutes) with no type annotation. TypeScript's excess-property check only fires on a FRESH object literal assigned directly to an annotated target; here the literal is assigned to an inferred `const`, and `createBrowserRouter(routeTable)` at line 31 then receives a non-fresh variable, so the check is skipped entirely at both ends. The result is that a typo in any route key is accepted by the compiler and only shows up as broken navigation at runtime. PROVEN: a probe reproducing this exact shape against the repo's real react-router — with `errorElment` instead of `errorElement`, `elemnt` instead of `element`, and `pathh` instead of `path` — compiles with zero errors under `strict: true`; annotating the same literal `: RouteObject[]` reports all three as TS2561 'Did you mean to write ...'. Consequences of each silent typo are severe and silent in kind: a misspelled `errorElement` means the app has no error boundary at all (the very thing ErrorBoundary.tsx exists for), a misspelled `element` renders a blank route, and a misspelled `path` means the route never matches and users get a 404 on a link that looks correct in source.

findings.title: Second, uncovered instance of the FileReader-result assertion — this one feeds the Gemini request body
findings.description: F004 covers the FileReader assertion in ProfileView. This is the same pattern in a file no lot covered, and it is on the PDF-upload path. `FileReader.result` is typed `string | ArrayBuffer | null` by lib.dom precisely because the same object serves readAsArrayBuffer; asserting `as string` removes the compiler's only reason to make the caller think about it. The unchecked `[1]` index compounds it: `split(',')[1]` is really `string | undefined` and only types as `string` because `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is off, so `resolve(base64)` satisfies `Promise<string>` while potentially resolving `undefined`. The value goes straight to `summarizePdf(base64Data: string)` and into the Gemini request as `inlineData.data`, where a malformed value produces an opaque SDK error rather than a local one. There is also no size check despite the UI text promising a 10MB maximum, so an arbitrarily large file is base64-inflated in memory and posted.

findings.title: AddBookModal gates `priority` on status but not `rating`, so every Want-to-Read book is persisted with a phantom rating of 4 that the export and the status toggle both treat as real
findings.description: CONSTRUCTIBLE IMPOSSIBLE STATE: a Book with `status: 'Want to Read'` and `rating: 4` that the user never rated. `Book.status` decides which of `rating` and `priority` is meaningful — the modal knows this, because it shows the rating input only when `status === 'Finished'` (line 149) and the priority select only otherwise (line 167), and it correctly writes `priority: status === 'Want to Read' ? priority : undefined` (line 75). It then writes `rating` unconditionally on the very next line up (line 74), taking the value straight from `useState(4)` (line 32) — a field the user was never shown. `Book.rating: number` (types.ts:36) records no relationship to `status`, so the compiler cannot see the asymmetry. CONSUMERS THAT MISHANDLE IT: (1) markdown.ts:14 emits `**Rating:** ${book.rating}/5` unconditionally, so both the per-book export (BookDetail.tsx:417) and the whole-library Markdown backup (ProfileView.tsx:89) state 'Rating: 4/5' for books the user has not read. (2) BookDetail.tsx:215 `rating: newStatus === 'Finished' ? book.rating || 5 : book.rating` — marking that book finished keeps the phantom 4 rather than prompting, at which point StatsView.tsx:18-20 folds it into the average rating over finished books, permanently skewing the headline stat with a number the user never entered. BookCard.tsx:97 and BookDetail.tsx:268 both gate the display on `status === 'Finished'`, which is why this is invisible in the UI and only surfaces in the export and after a status flip. DISTINCT FROM PRIOR FINDINGS: F061 is about `rating: 0` conflating 'unrated' with 'rated zero' at StatsView:20, and RT-F008 is about the Goodreads parser's `0` sentinel; this is the opposite failure — a non-zero rating fabricated by the add-book UI for a status where the field has no meaning.

findings.title: togglePlay ignores the Promise returned by play() — the same call is caught 21 lines above — and flips isPlaying unconditionally, so the UI shows Pause while nothing is playing
findings.description: `HTMLMediaElement.play()` is declared `Promise<void>` and rejects routinely: NotAllowedError when autoplay policy blocks a gesture-less play, AbortError when `src` changes mid-load, NotSupportedError on a bad blob URL. The file already knows this — line 29 attaches `.catch((e) => console.error('Autoplay failed', e))` to the identical call. `togglePlay` at lines 45-54 does not, so the rejection is unhandled. Worse, `setIsPlaying(!isPlaying)` on line 52 runs regardless of whether playback actually started, so the type-level 'this succeeded' assumption leaks into state: the button renders the Pause icon and the progress bar sits at 0 while nothing plays, and the user has no way to tell the difference from a stalled stream. Exact input: a generated WAV whose blob URL has already been revoked, or any environment where the play attempt is rejected. Broken consumer: the AudioPlayer's own render (lines 190-194), which trusts `isPlaying`.
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the state follow the outcome rather than the intention: `audioRef.current.play().then(() => setIsPlaying(true)).catch(() => setIsPlaying(false))` on line 50, and move the `setIsPlaying(!isPlaying)` on line 52 into the pause branch only. The existing `onPlay`/`onPause` handlers (lines 117-118) already sync state from the element, so this mainly removes the optimistic flip. Risk: none — the element's own events remain the source of truth.

findings.title: Chat Message has no error variant, so a failure is rendered as if the assistant said it — and if the stream already emitted one chunk, the error is dropped entirely
findings.description: CONSTRUCTIBLE IMPOSSIBLE STATE: a `Message` with `role: 'model'` whose `text` is an AiError string rather than model output. `interface Message { role: 'user' | 'model'; text: string }` (lines 15-18) has no third arm and no status field, so the catch block at 70-79 has nowhere to put a failure and overwrites the streaming placeholder's text instead. TWO DISTINCT CONSUMER FAILURES, both reachable: (1) When the request fails before any chunk arrives (no API key, offline, 429), the placeholder's text is replaced with `toAiError(err).message` and the renderer at lines 140-152 paints it in the orange assistant bubble behind the Sparkles avatar, styled identically to a real answer — the user cannot distinguish 'Could not reach Google. Check your connection and try again.' from something the book assistant asserted. (2) Worse, when the stream fails *after* emitting at least one chunk, the replace predicate `entry.role === 'model' && entry.text === ''` (line 75) no longer matches — the placeholder's text is non-empty by then — so `.map` returns the array unchanged and the error message is silently discarded. `sendMessageStream` (chat.ts:29-38) calls `onChunk(text)` inside the `for await` loop and rethrows anything the iterator raises, so a mid-stream safety block or dropped connection lands exactly here. `isLoading` then flips false in the `finally` and the user is left looking at a truncated half-sentence with no indication anything went wrong. The type gives no hint that `text` carries two different kinds of value.
findings.suggestedPatch: Smallest first step, contained entirely in ChatModal.tsx: add the missing arm to the local type — `type Message = { role: 'user'; text: string } | { role: 'model'; text: string; failed?: true }` — then in the catch, drop the `entry.text === ''` predicate and replace the last model entry with `{ ...entry, text: entry.text ? entry.text + '\n\n' + message : message, failed: true }`, and in the renderer branch on `msg.failed` to use the error styling the app already has (the red panel at ApiKeyDialog.tsx:66 is the existing precedent). `Message` is declared locally and used nowhere else in the repo, so this touches one file and no other producer or consumer.

findings.title: pages is inferred string[] but .filter(Boolean) can yield an empty array, so pages[currentPage] is undefined while typed string and crashes RenderFormattedContent
findings.description:
The `pages` useMemo is inferred as `string[]`, and the `['No content available.']` fallback on line 183 shows the author intended a non-empty guarantee. The guarantee does not hold: the fallback only fires when `detailedSummary` is falsy, so a whitespace-only `detailedSummary` passes the check and then `.map(s => s.trim()).filter(Boolean)` reduces it to `[]` (verified in node). With `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` off, `pages[currentPage]` at line 395 is typed `string` while holding `undefined`, and it is handed to `RenderFormattedContent`'s required `content: string` prop, whose first statement is `content.split('
')` -> `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'split')` (verified). Exact input: a `detailedSummary` of `'   '` or `'

'`. That is reachable because `generateDetailedSummary` (summarize.ts:99) returns `text || 'Failed to...'` — a whitespace-only stream is truthy, so it is returned and persisted verbatim as a real deep-dive. Broken consumer: ReaderPage -> EReader throws during render, and react-router's errorElement replaces the whole app; the progress bar on line 457 also divides by `pages.length` of 0.
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the non-empty guarantee real at line 189: `return sections.length > 0 ? sections : ['No content available.'];`. Optionally also clamp the index at line 395 (`pages[Math.min(currentPage, pages.length - 1)] ?? ''`) so a shrinking `pages` from a summary update cannot leave `currentPage` past the end. Risk: none — it is a one-line widening of an existing fallback.

findings.title: profileId and bookId are freely interchangeable across the review-card path, and QuizModal has both wrong calls one keystroke away on adjacent lines
findings.description: COMPILING-WRONG-CALLS, both in the same effect. (1) `reviewCards.listByProfile(profileId: string)` (repo.ts:78) and `reviewCards.listByBook(bookId: string)` (repo.ts:94) are adjacent methods on the same object with byte-identical signatures `(x: string) => Promise<ReviewCard[]>`. Line 49 calls `reviewCards.listByBook(book.id)`; changing it to `reviewCards.listByProfile(book.id)` type-checks, returns `[]` because no card's `profileId` is ever a book id, and so the `seen` dedupe set is empty forever — every quiz retake re-inserts every question as a fresh card with a fresh `crypto.randomUUID()`, growing the reviewCards store without bound and flooding the review queue with duplicates. Nothing throws; the only symptom is a review deck that keeps growing. (2) Five lines later, `newCard({ profileId: book.profileId, bookId: book.id, ... })` puts the two most confusable values in the app on consecutive lines of one object literal. `NewCardInput.profileId` and `NewCardInput.bookId` are both `string` (srs.ts:14-15), as are `Book.profileId` and `Book.id` (types.ts:29-30), so transposing them satisfies the type exactly. CONSUMER THAT MISHANDLES IT: `useReviewQueue` calls `cardRepo.listDue(profile.id)` (useReviewQueue.ts:20), which filters `card.profileId === profileId` (repo.ts:80) — transposed cards are never due for anyone, so the Review page shows 'Nothing due' permanently while the store fills up, and `reviewCards.removeByBook` (repo.ts:104) can never reclaim them either because it matches on `card.bookId`. WHY THERE IS NO RUNTIME BACKSTOP: both values are `crypto.randomUUID()` output (repo.ts:4), and the reviewCards store's only index is `['profileId', 'dueAt']` (db.ts:38) with no foreign-key constraint, so a card pointing at a profile that is really a book is a perfectly valid record. DISTINCT FROM RT-F101: that finding is about the `DBSchema` declaration being an unvalidated assertion over IndexedDB contents; this is about the two id kinds being mutually assignable in the repo's own public surface.
findings.suggestedPatch: Smallest first step that actually removes the hazard, without a repo-wide brand migration: give the two lookups shapes that are not mutually assignable. Change `reviewCards.listByProfile` / `listByBook` to take a single tagged argument — `listBy(scope: { profileId: string } | { bookId: string })` — so `listBy({ bookId: book.id })` cannot be mistaken for the profile lookup and the wrong call stops compiling. That is one method in repo.ts plus its four call sites (QuizModal.tsx:49, useReviewQueue via listDue, repo.ts:86 and repo.ts:106) and the repo tests. HONEST NOTE ON THE FULLER FIX: branding `ProfileId` and `BookId` outright would also catch case (2) — the transposed `newCard` literal, which a tagged-argument change does not reach — but that genuinely does require touching every producer and consumer of both ids (repo.ts, useLibrary, useBookRoute, QuizModal, srs.ts, migrate.ts, AppShell, the LibraryExport round-trip, plus `as BookId` escapes where ids re-enter from `useParams` and from imported JSON). Recommend the tagged lookup now and the brand as a scoped structural item, not as part of this audit's apply wave.

findings.title: useBookRoute returns a book and a summary as independent values, and every direct book-to-book navigation commits a render where the summary belongs to the previous book
findings.description: CONSTRUCTIBLE IMPOSSIBLE STATE: `summary.bookId !== book.id`. `book` is derived synchronously from the route param on every render (line 13, `books.find(c => c.id === id)`), while `summary` is a `useState` slot written asynchronously by the effect at line 21. React Router renders the same `BookDetailPage` element for `book/:id` at the same tree position, so a /book/A -> /book/B navigation re-renders rather than remounts and the `summary` state survives. That means at least one committed frame has `book = B` and `summary = SummaryOf(A)`. HOW IT IS REACHED: the DailyWisdomModal is mounted in AppShell above the Outlet, so it can fire while the user is already on /book/A; its `onReadMore` calls `navigate('/book/' + dailyBook.id)` (AppShell.tsx:213) — a direct book-to-book navigation. Browser Back/Forward between two book pages does the same. CONSUMERS THAT MISHANDLE IT: (1) BookDetail renders `book.title` and `book.author` from the new book alongside `summary.oneSentenceTakeaway` (line 452), `summary.summary` (461), `summary.keyInsights` (470) and `summary.actionableSteps` (490) from the old one — the reader sees book B's title over book A's content. (2) Worse, the pair is a write source, not just a render source: `BookDetail.handleMasterclassClick` (BookDetail.tsx:184-187) captures the current `summary` for the whole duration of a streaming `generateDetailedSummary` call, then calls `onSummaryUpdate({ ...summary, detailedSummary })`, which BookDetailPage.tsx:44-46 forwards to `saveSummary`. `saveSummary` resolves the target book by `bookRepo.get(summary.bookId)` (useLibrary.tsx:81) — so a deep dive started on A and landing after a navigation to B is written onto A's summary while the page shows B, and B's reader then opens on 'No content available.' The type system permits all of this because `Book` and `Summary` are two unrelated values in an untagged bag; nothing expresses that they must agree on an id. HONEST SCOPE: the guaranteed part of this is the render-frame mismatch (short, but committed and painted); the persistent write to the wrong record needs an in-flight deep dive across the navigation.
findings.suggestedPatch: Smallest first step: make the pair inseparable rather than adding a tag. Replace the two independent slots with one, keyed by the book it belongs to — `const [loaded, setLoaded] = useState<{ bookId: string; summary: Summary | undefined } | null>(null)` — set it as `setLoaded({ bookId: book.id, summary: s })` inside the effect, and return `summary: loaded?.bookId === book?.id ? loaded.summary : undefined`. That is a ~6-line change confined to useBookRoute.ts; both consumers already accept `Summary | undefined`, so BookDetail and EReader need no edit and will simply show their existing not-yet-summarised states for the mismatched frame instead of the wrong book's text. Add a cancellation guard in the same effect (`let cancelled = false` / `if (!cancelled) setLoaded(...)`, the pattern ProfileContext.tsx:28 already uses) so a late resolution cannot overwrite a newer book. Does NOT require touching every producer and consumer.

findings.title: The recommendation cache is asserted out of localStorage and the only check is one a string also passes
findings.description: The home page reads a cross-session localStorage value and asserts it to `{ at: number; items: Recommendation[] }`. The single guard is `parsed.items?.length`, which is a truthiness check on `.length` — it passes for a non-empty string, for an array of nulls, and for an array of numbers. `setRecommendations(parsed.items)` then hands it to `RecommendationCarousel`, whose props declare `Recommendation[]` and which immediately does `recommendations.map(rec => ...)` and reads `rec.title` (as the React key), `rec.coverUrl` (as an ``) and `rec.description`. A cached `items` of `"stale"` throws 'recommendations.map is not a function' during render; `[null]` throws on `rec.title`. Either takes out the library route via the router ErrorBoundary, and because the bad value is persisted the failure repeats on every reload until the user clears storage — the try/catch at line 39 only covers the parse, not the render. The writer at line 74 stores `getAIRecommendations()` output, which is itself an unvalidated model response (F030), so the cache is downstream of an already-erased boundary.
findings.suggestedPatch:
Export a guard next to the type (`src/features/library/recommendationDefaults.ts` is the natural home since RECS_CACHE_KEY already lives there):
```ts
export const isRecommendation = (v: unknown): v is Recommendation =>
  typeof v === 'object' && v !== null &&
  ['title','author','description','coverUrl'].every(k => typeof (v as Record<string, unknown>)[k] === 'string');
```
Then parse to `unknown` and narrow: `const parsed: unknown = JSON.parse(cached);` followed by an object check, `typeof parsed.at === 'number'`, `Array.isArray(parsed.items)` and `parsed.items.filter(isRecommendation)`; if the filtered list is empty, remove the key and fall through to RECOMMENDED_BOOKS. Risk: none — the defaults array is already the fallback, so a rejected cache degrades to the shipped recommendations.

findings.title: The priority sort table is Record<string, number> instead of Record<Priority, number>, so a mis-keyed or renamed priority silently degrades the sort and the ?? 1 that catches it is invisible to the compiler
findings.description: COMPILING-WRONG-VALUE: `priorityScore` is declared `Record<string, number>`, so its keys are unchecked. Writing `{ Hgih: 3, Medium: 2, Low: 1 }`, or renaming a member of the `Priority` union in types.ts:2 without updating this literal, type-checks cleanly and silently collapses every Want-to-Read book to the same score — the queue stops being priority-ordered and falls through to date order with no error anywhere. Declaring it `Record<Priority, number>` would make both mistakes compile errors, and costs one word. THE SECOND HALF IS ALREADY LIVE: because the index signature is `string`, `priorityScore[a.priority || 'Low']` is typed `number` and can never be `undefined` as far as the compiler is concerned — which makes the `?? 1` on lines 57-58 provably dead code by the types. It is not dead at runtime. `Book.priority?: Priority` is not validated at either of its two ingress points: migrate.ts:111 copies `legacy.priority` out of a `readJson<LegacyBook>` cast over raw localStorage (migrate.ts:54-61), and useLibrary.importLibrary (useLibrary.tsx:111) copies it out of a hand-editable backup file. So a stored `priority: 'urgent'` is representable, reaches this lookup, misses, and is rescued only by a fallback the type system says is unnecessary — `eslint --fix` with `no-unnecessary-condition` enabled, or any reviewer trusting the declared type, would remove it and turn a silent mis-sort into `NaN` propagating through the comparator. CONSUMER THAT MISHANDLES THE SAME VALUE: BookCard.tsx:69-75 renders `{book.priority}` verbatim while `getPriorityColor(p?: string)` falls through its `switch` to the `default` arm, so that record paints a badge reading 'urgent' in the blue Low styling. DISTINCT FROM RT-F108: that finding covers the `e.target.value as Priority` assertion in AddBookModal as a producer; this is the weak Record type at the consumer that hides the miss, in a different file.
findings.suggestedPatch: Two-token fix, one file, no ripple: change line 56 to `const priorityScore: Record<Priority, number> = { High: 3, Medium: 2, Low: 1 };` (`Priority` is already imported into this module's type graph via `types.ts`; add it to the existing `import type { BookStatus }` on line 14). The compiler then rejects a typo'd or renamed key, and — because the index type is now the union — `priorityScore[a.priority || 'Low']` remains `number`, so the `?? 1` stays syntactically valid while the real guard moves to compile time. Hoist the literal out of the comparator while you are there; it is currently reallocated for every comparison. This does NOT fix the unvalidated ingress at migrate.ts:111 / importLibrary — that needs a `isPriority()` guard at those two boundaries, which is a separate ~8-line change and is the honest prerequisite for trusting `Book.priority` as a union at all.

findings.title: addBook is the one site that mints a summary id and a book id together, and swapping them type-checks and leaves no runtime trace
findings.description: COMPILING-WRONG-CALL: `Summary.id` and `Summary.bookId` are both bare `string` (types.ts:55-56) and `Book.id` is bare `string` (types.ts:29). At useLibrary.tsx:48 both values are in scope at once, so writing `await summaryRepo.upsert({ ...options.summary, id: book.id, bookId: summaryId })` — the two identifiers transposed — satisfies `Summary` exactly and `npx tsc --noEmit` stays at exit 0. WHY IT IS UNDETECTABLE AT RUNTIME TOO: every id in the system comes from `crypto.randomUUID()` (repo.ts:4 `newId`, useLibrary.tsx:44, srs.ts:24, toastStore.ts:17), so both values are indistinguishable v4 UUIDs — no length check, no prefix, no assertion, and no IndexedDB constraint can catch the swap. CONSUMER THAT MISHANDLES IT: `summaries.getByBook(bookId)` (repo.ts:112) reads the `by-book` index, so it would return `undefined` for the book forever, while `Book.summaryId` still points at a stored record — which is precisely the 'summarised but no summary' contradiction F050/F011/F012 already document as a visible UI failure, arriving here as silent write-time corruption instead. `books.remove` (repo.ts:68-70) resolves the orphan via `getByBook` too, so it would never delete it. CORROBORATION THAT THIS CONFUSION IS ALREADY LIVE: ProfileView.tsx:88 builds `const summaryById = new Map(data.summaries.map((s) => [s.bookId, s]))` — a map named 'ById' that is keyed by *book* id. Correcting the map to match its own name compiles (both fields are `string`) and makes `summaryById.get(b.id)` return `undefined` for every book, at which point `libraryToMarkdown` silently writes 'Not summarised yet.' (markdown.ts:19-20) for the entire library export with no error. HONEST SCOPE: no call site is wrong today; this is a latent foot-gun, and it is reported because the failure mode is silent, unrecoverable data corruption with zero runtime signal — the exact profile the spec says branded types are worth paying for.
findings.suggestedPatch: Smallest first step that pays off, and it is genuinely small because the ids have exactly one producer: in src/lib/storage/repo.ts add `export type BookId = string & { readonly __brand: 'BookId' }` and `SummaryId`, retype `newId` to a generic `const newId = <T extends string>() => crypto.randomUUID() as T`, and brand only the three fields that actually collide — `Book.id: BookId`, `Summary.id: SummaryId`, `Summary.bookId: BookId`. HONEST RETROFIT COST: branding `Book.id` alone touches every producer and consumer of a book id (useLibrary, useBookRoute, BookDetail/BookDetailPage, QuizModal, blobs.*, reviewCards.*, migrate.ts, the LibraryExport round-trip and the repo tests) and will need `as BookId` at the two boundaries where ids come back from JSON (`importLibrary`) and from the route param (`useParams`). If that is too much, the strictly-cheaper 90% fix is to stop having the two values in scope together: change `AddBookOptions.summary` to be written by a single repo helper `summaries.createFor(book, draft)` that mints the id itself, so useLibrary never holds both a summary id and a book id at the same time. That is a ~10-line change in one file and removes the swap opportunity outright.

findings.title: importGoodreadsRows declares Promise<{added, duplicates}> as if it always resolves, and its only caller uses try/finally with no catch, so a quota failure part-way through a large import is swallowed entirely
findings.description: `importGoodreadsRows(rows): Promise<{ added: number; duplicates: number }>` claims it always resolves to a count. It writes one IndexedDB record per row in a loop (line 150) with no transaction and no error handling, so `bookRepo.create` can reject with QuotaExceededError or an aborted transaction mid-loop — most likely on exactly the workload the project invariants call out ('Importing a large library must stay free'). The declared type gives the caller no signal that this can fail. Broken consumer: GoodreadsImport.tsx:35-48 wraps the call in `try { ... } finally { setIsImporting(false) }` with NO catch, and the call site is `onClick={() => void handleImport()}` (line 97), so the rejection becomes an unhandled promise rejection: no toast, no error boundary, `onDone()` never fires so the modal stays open, and the spinner just stops. The user is left with a partially imported library and zero indication that anything went wrong, while the already-written books have silently landed.
findings.suggestedPatch: Widen the contract to report partial success: return `{ added: number; duplicates: number; failed: number }` and wrap the per-row `bookRepo.create` at line 150 in try/catch so one rejected write increments `failed` instead of aborting. Add a `catch` beside the `finally` at GoodreadsImport.tsx:45 that raises `toast.error('Import stopped partway — some books may not have been saved.')`. Risk: the success toast copy at GoodreadsImport.tsx:40-43 and goodreadsImport.test.tsx assertions need updating for the new field.

findings.title: Vitest's `stubGlobal(value: unknown)` plus a bare `vi.fn()` means the matchMedia and fetch mocks are checked against nothing
findings.description: Two vendor escape hatches compose here. node_modules/vitest/dist/index.d.ts:588 declares `stubGlobal: (name: string | symbol | number, value: unknown) => VitestUtils` — the replacement value is `unknown`, so it is never compared to the global it replaces. node_modules/@vitest/spy/dist/index.d.ts:151 declares `type Procedure = (...args: any[]) => any` as the default type argument of `Mock<T>`, so a bare `vi.fn()` accepts any implementation and returns `any` from every call. `mockPrefersDark` uses both: `vi.fn()` with no type argument, `.mockImplementation` with a hand-rolled return shape, and `stubGlobal` to install it as `window.matchMedia`. Nothing checks that shape against `(query: string) => MediaQueryList`. PROVEN: under `strict: true` a probe compiles `vi.stubGlobal('matchMedia', 12345)`, `vi.stubGlobal('fetch', { not: 'a function' })`, `vi.fn().mockImplementation((wrongParam: number) => ({ typo_matches: wrongParam }))`, and `vi.fn()('anything', 999).does.not.exist()` — all with zero errors. This matters because this mock is the only thing standing between useTheme's system-preference branch and reality: useTheme.ts:11 reads `.matches` and useTheme.ts:23-24 call `query.addEventListener?.('change', ...)` with optional chaining, so a mock that silently lost `addEventListener` or renamed `matches` would make the tests pass while the feature broke. Per the spec, a fixture that does not match the real shape means the test is exercising a fake. The same `unknown` hole is used for `fetch` at src/lib/covers/index.test.ts:6 and :68, src/features/library/goodreadsImport.test.tsx:85, and src/test/smoke.test.tsx:47 — those three do at least annotate the implementation's parameter as `RequestInfo | URL`, which is the pattern to copy.
findings.suggestedPatch: Close the hole where it enters by giving `vi.fn` its real type argument, which makes the return shape checkable: `vi.fn<(query: string) => MediaQueryList>().mockImplementation((query) => ({ ... }) as MediaQueryList)` — or better, drop the cast and let the object literal be checked directly by typing the helper's return: `function fakeMediaQueryList(query: string, matches: boolean): MediaQueryList { return { matches, media: query, onchange: null, addEventListener: vi.fn(), removeEventListener: vi.fn(), addListener: vi.fn(), removeListener: vi.fn(), dispatchEvent: vi.fn() }; }` then `vi.stubGlobal('matchMedia', vi.fn<typeof window.matchMedia>(() => fakeMediaQueryList(...)))`. Because `stubGlobal` will always take `unknown`, the durable fix is a single typed test helper (e.g. `src/test/globals.ts` exporting `stubMatchMedia(matches: boolean)` and `stubFetch(handler)`) that owns the one unchecked `stubGlobal` call and exposes a strictly-typed face to the five test files — the spec's isolation prescription applied to the test harness.

findings.title: The universal error normaliser asserts `unknown` to an object and crashes on two of the values JS can throw
findings.description: `statusOf` reads `.status` off a value typed `unknown` by asserting it to `{ status?: unknown }`. Verified in node: this throws TypeError for `null` and for `undefined` (a thrown string or number is fine). F029 covers line 53's substring-matching of the error message; this is a different defect on a different line — an assertion that removes the compiler's protection over a property read. It matters more than it looks because of where it sits: `toAiError` is documented as 'Normalises anything thrown by the Gemini SDK or fetch', it is the sole error funnel for the whole app (8 call sites including `AppShell.handleAiError`, which every feature routes through), and the whole point of the function is to be total over `unknown`. When it is not, a throw of `null`/`undefined` — `Promise.reject()` with no argument, a `throw null` from any dependency, an aborted operation — converts a handled error path into an unhandled crash inside the handler, which is strictly worse than the original failure. The `unknown` parameter type is correct; the assertion is what discards it.

findings.title: getAIRecommendations declares Promise<Recommendation[]> with four required strings but builds them from an unvalidated cast, then the values are round-tripped through localStorage and re-asserted
findings.description: `Recommendation` (lines 9-14) requires `title`, `author`, `description` and `coverUrl` to all be present strings. They come from `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as { recommendations?: Omit[] }` with no element validation, and the values then make a second unvalidated trip: LibraryPage.tsx:76 serialises them into localStorage and LibraryPage.tsx:35 reads them back as `JSON.parse(cached) as { at: number; items: Recommendation[] }`, where the only check is `parsed.items?.length`. So a stale cache entry written by an older version, or a hand-edited localStorage value, re-enters typed code as fully-populated Recommendations. Exact input: the model omits `title` for one entry. Broken consumers: `fetchCover(rec.title, rec.author)` at line 37 bottoms out in `placeholderCover(title)` which calls `title.trim()` -> TypeError (caught here, so the whole refresh degrades to a toast); RecommendationCarousel.tsx:81 uses `key={rec.title}` so React keys collide on undefined; coverFallback (line 19) calls the same `placeholderCover(rec.title)` from an `` handler where there is no try/catch at all; and LibraryPage.tsx:90 forwards the undefined title into `summarizeBook(rec.title, rec.author)`, producing a prompt about a book named 'undefined'.
findings.suggestedPatch: Filter at line 35: `(data.recommendations ?? []).filter((r) => typeof r?.title === 'string' && r.title.trim() !== '' && typeof r?.author === 'string')` before the map. Apply the same predicate to `parsed.items` at LibraryPage.tsx:36 so a stale or edited cache cannot re-enter typed code. Risk: none — LibraryPage.tsx:72 already no-ops on an empty result and falls back to RECOMMENDED_BOOKS.

findings.title: toGenerated promises a fully-formed Book and Summary but its `??` and `||` defaults only guard null/undefined, so a wrong-typed model field is persisted as a real summary
findings.description: `toGenerated(...): GeneratedBook` declares `keyInsights: string[]`, `actionableSteps: string[]`, `rating: number` and `readingTimeMinutes: number` as guaranteed. Its inputs come from `JSON.parse(response.text || '{}') as RawBookResponse` (lines 52 and 73). `RawBookResponse` is honest about ABSENCE — every field is optional, with a comment explaining why — but says nothing about WRONG TYPE, and `??`/`||` only substitute for null/undefined. A model that returns `keyInsights` as a single string rather than an array, or `rating` as `"4"`, passes straight through: `data.keyInsights ?? []` keeps the string. The result is written to IndexedDB as a real `Summary` by useLibrary.addBook -> summaryRepo.upsert. Broken consumers: BookDetail.tsx:470 runs `(summary?.keyInsights ?? []).map(...)` — `.map` is not a function on a string, so the book detail route throws to the error boundary every time that book is opened; markdown.ts:24-25 does `keyInsights.length > 0` (a string passes) then `.map` and throws the same way, killing Markdown export. This is the same file as the already-known sentinel at line 99 but a distinct defect at lines 22-41, and unlike that one it corrupts stored data rather than just labelling it.

findings.title: base64ToBytes is typed as total over every string but throws DOMException on any input that is not valid base64, and one of its two callers feeds it untrusted localStorage
findings.description: `base64ToBytes(base64: string): Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer>` declares totality over the whole `string` domain. `atob` throws `DOMException: Invalid character` for any string whose length or alphabet is wrong (verified in node), so the function is partial and the signature says otherwise. Caller 1 — tts.ts:30 — passes a Gemini response and sits inside a try/catch that maps the throw to an AiError, so it is handled. Caller 2 — migrate.ts:136 and :142 — passes `legacy.pdfData` and `legacy.audioData` read verbatim out of localStorage, which is user-editable, survives across app versions, and (per CLAUDE.md) held the multi-megabyte base64 blobs that 'broke the original app', so truncated values are the expected failure. That call site has no try/catch, which is the mechanism behind RT-F002's permanent spinner. Reporting it separately because the fix belongs in base64.ts: a `(string) => Uint8Array` that can reject routine input should say so in its type rather than relying on every caller to remember.
findings.suggestedPatch: Add a sibling `tryBase64ToBytes(base64: string): Uint8Array<ArrayBuffer> | null` that wraps the `atob` call in try/catch and returns null, and use it at migrate.ts:136 and :142 so an unreadable legacy blob is skipped instead of aborting the migration. Leave `base64ToBytes` for the tts.ts path but document the throw in a JSDoc `@throws`. Risk: none — additive, and the tts.ts caller is unchanged.

findings.title: parseGoodreadsCsv returns 'Unknown' and 0 as not-found sentinels typed as real author and rating values, and StatsView averages the 0s into the user's rating, silently deflating it
findings.description: `GoodreadsRow.author: string` and `rating: number` (lines 5-7) claim every row carries a real author and a real rating. The parser manufactures sentinels for the missing case: line 109 substitutes the literal string `'Unknown'` for a blank author cell, and line 111 substitutes `0` for a missing or unparseable 'My Rating' — which is exactly what Goodreads writes for a book you read but never rated. Nothing downstream distinguishes sentinel from datum, because the types cannot express the difference. Exact input: a real Goodreads export in which some read books are unrated (the common case). Broken consumer: useLibrary.tsx:156 persists `rating: row.rating` as a genuine Book rating with `status: 'Finished'`, and StatsView.tsx:18-20 computes `finished.reduce((acc, b) => acc + b.rating, 0) / finished.length` over ALL finished books — so every unrated import drags the displayed average rating toward zero, with no indication why. BookCard.tsx:100 also renders a confident '0/5' badge for those books. The same sentinel is minted a second time at migrate.ts:113 (`rating: legacy.rating ?? 0`), so it travels in a pack.

findings.title: `readJson<T>` is a generic assertion factory: one `as T` that manufactures a fully-trusted type for every caller and hides from any `as`-grep
findings.description: Filed for the assertion-laundering angle only; the boundary/validation aspect of localStorage ingress is owned by another class and is not re-reported here. `readJson<T>(key): T | null` has an entirely unconstrained type parameter whose only binding is `JSON.parse(raw) as T` on line 58. `JSON.parse` returns `any` (confirmed by a compiler-API pass over the repo: it is one of only six expressions in all of src/** whose inferred type is `any`), and the function's sole job is to convert that `any` into whatever the caller names, with no runtime check of any kind. The effect on this audit's own census is the point: the cast count for this file is 1, but the number of unvalidated type claims is the number of call sites — migrate.ts:89 asserts a `LegacyProfile` and migrate.ts:99 asserts a `LegacyBook[]`, and neither line contains the word `as`, so neither appears in any assertion inventory. A helper like this makes the codebase look cleaner than it is and grows the risk silently as callers are added. The values it produces are consumed immediately and structurally: line 99's result is iterated with `for (const legacy of legacyBooks)`, which throws TypeError if the stored JSON was an object rather than an array; line 91 reads `legacyProfile?.name?.trim()`, which throws if `name` was stored as a number. The declared `LegacyBook`/`LegacyProfile` interfaces make every field optional, which reads as careful design but is undermined by the fact that nothing establishes the top-level shape at all.
findings.suggestedPatch: Make the helper honest about what it actually knows and push the assertion to the two sites that can reason about it. Minimal, no new dependency: change the signature to `function readJson(key: string): unknown` (drop the type parameter and the `as T`), then narrow at each caller with a two-line guard — line 99 becomes `const raw = readJson(key); const legacyBooks: LegacyBook[] = Array.isArray(raw) ? raw : [];` and line 89 becomes `const raw = readJson(key); const legacyProfile = (raw && typeof raw === 'object' && !Array.isArray(raw)) ? (raw as LegacyProfile) : null;`. That turns two invisible lies into two visible, greppable assertions each guarded by a real runtime check, converts the current TypeError-on-corrupt-storage into a clean skip, and costs about six lines. Do NOT keep `readJson<T>` and merely rename it — an unconstrained `<T>` over `JSON.parse` is the pattern itself.

findings.title: crypto.randomUUID() is typed as always available but is secure-context-only; every id in the app depends on it
findings.description: This is a platform-API boundary, not one of the `as`-cast cluster the prior findings enumerate. lib.dom declares `Crypto.randomUUID(): \`${string}-${string}-...\`` unconditionally, so the compiler guarantees availability. The runtime does not: `randomUUID` is a secure-context-only API, so on `http://` origins that are not localhost it is `undefined` and the call throws TypeError. That is not a theoretical origin for this app — the README's whole pitch is moving your library between devices, and `vite --host` on a LAN IP over plain http is the standard way to open a local-first app on a phone. In that context the failure is total, because the 5 call sites cover every write in the product: `repo.ts:4` (`newId`, used by profiles.create and books.create), `srs.ts:24` (every review card), `migrate.ts:102` (every migrated summary), `useLibrary.tsx:44` (every summary id) and `toastStore.ts:19` (every toast — so even the error message about the failure cannot render). Creating a profile is the very first action a new user takes, so the app is unusable rather than degraded.

findings.title: The env-var boundary is typed `any` by vite/client, so the repo's zero-`any` property has a hole nobody wrote
findings.description: The audit spec names env vars as a boundary explicitly, and no lot was assigned to it. There are currently zero `import.meta.env` / `process.env` usages in src — but the type that would govern them is already `any`. `tsconfig.json` lists `vite/client` in `types`, which loads `node_modules/vite/types/importMeta.d.ts`. Because that file's `ViteTypeOptions` leaves `strictImportMetaEnv` commented out, `ImportMetaEnvFallbackKey` resolves to `string` and `ImportMetaEnv extends Record<string, any>`. Empirically verified with a tsc probe against this repo's own vite and typescript: `IsAny<ImportMetaEnv['VITE_SOME_UNDECLARED_KEY']>` resolves to `true`, and `const oops: number = import.meta.env.VITE_X.trim().nope()` compiles with zero errors under `--strict`. So the moment anyone adds a feature flag or an analytics key, they get an unannounced `any` that flows anywhere, with no `any` keyword and no lint hit — and the project's headline invariant work around 'no key in the bundle' makes env vars a likely near-term addition. Vite ships the opt-in fix; this repo has not taken it.

Nothing throws — the wrong value just becomes permanent data. findings.title: `Promise.prototype.catch` contextually types its callback parameter as `any` — a second proven `noImplicitAny` escape hatch, from lib.es5
findings.description: Reported as the second confirmed instance of the class the `import.meta.env` finding opened, this time sourced from TypeScript's own standard library rather than a third-party package. `lib.es5.d.ts` declares `catch<TResult>(onrejected?: ((reason: any) => ...) | undefined | null)`, so the rejection reason is contextually typed `any`. An unannotated arrow-function parameter therefore lands on `any` with no error even though `noImplicitAny` is on — the flag only fires when TypeScript cannot infer a contextual type, and here it can, badly. A compiler-API sweep of all 86 source files found this to be the ONLY unannotated parameter in the repo whose inferred type is `any`, which is why the severity is low: the blast radius is one line and the value only reaches `console.error`. The finding's value is the pattern, not the instance — no lint rule in this project can catch it (the type-aware @typescript-eslint tier is inert for want of `parserOptions.project`), and the same hole reopens at every future `.catch(...)`, `.then(ok, err)`, `new Promise((res, rej) => ...)` (already present at src/components/AddBookModal.tsx:39, where `reject` is `(reason?: any) => void`) and any other lib.dom/lib.es5 callback typed with `any`. PROVEN: under `strict: true` a probe compiles `audio.play().catch((e) => { console.error(e.message.toUpperCase().nope()); const n: number = e; return n; })` with zero errors.
findings.suggestedPatch: Annotate the parameter: `.catch((e: unknown) => console.error('Autoplay failed', e))`. `unknown` is the correct type here rather than a cop-out — a promise rejection genuinely can be anything, and nothing downstream needs to narrow it because `console.error` accepts `unknown`. Systemically, the durable fix is the one already filed against the ESLint config: adding `parserOptions.projectService` turns on `@typescript-eslint/no-unsafe-argument` / `no-unsafe-member-access` / `no-unsafe-assignment`, which are the only tooling in this stack that can see library-sourced `any` at all. Without them, `noImplicitAny` will keep reporting a clean bill of health on exactly the cases it cannot see.

findings.title: An unvalidated MIME string read out of IndexedDB reaches a same-origin script-execution sink
findings.description: `blobs.get` reconstructs a Blob from a stored record with `new Blob([record.bytes], { type: record.type })` (repo.ts:144). `record.type` is declared `string` by StoredBlob and is never validated on read — db.ts's schema is the only thing asserting it exists at all. `handleOpenPdf` then does `URL.createObjectURL(pdf)` and `window.open(url, '_blank')`. A blob: URL inherits the creating page's origin, so if `record.type` were ever `text/html` the opened document would execute script with full access to this origin's IndexedDB and localStorage — which holds the user's Gemini API key. Being honest about reachability: no current writer can poison it. `blobs.put` takes `blob.type` from a File the user picked and AddBookModal requires `type === 'application/pdf'`; migrate.ts passes the literals `'application/pdf'` and `'audio/wav'`; and blobs are deliberately excluded from LibraryExport, so the untrusted import path cannot reach them. The finding is that the type system provides no barrier at all if a future writer is added (a blob-carrying backup format is a natural next feature), and that the sink is one line from the read.
findings.suggestedPatch: Pin the MIME at the read boundary rather than trusting the record: in repo.ts, map BlobKind to an allowed type and use it — `const MIME: Record<BlobKind, string> = { pdf: 'application/pdf', 'audio-short': 'audio/wav', 'audio-long': 'audio/wav' };` then `new Blob([record.bytes], { type: MIME[kind] })`. The kind is already a parameter, so nothing at the call sites changes and the stored `type` field becomes advisory. Also `URL.revokeObjectURL(url)` after the open (BookDetail.tsx:199 and the two AudioPlayer track URLs leak object URLs for the page's lifetime). Risk: a record stored with an unexpected MIME would now open under the pinned one — acceptable, since only these three kinds exist.

findings.title: Index-site assertions that are no-ops today and would pre-suppress `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` tomorrow
findings.description: `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is off, so `items[0]` is already typed `HTMLElement` and `bytes[i]` is already `number`. PROVEN by probe: the identical code with the `!` and the `as number` removed compiles clean under the repo's exact flags — all three assertions are currently doing nothing at all. Their real effect is deferred. The tsconfig gap for `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is one of the flags this audit is expected to recommend enabling, and these three sites are precisely the ones that would silently survive it: PROVEN by a second probe compiled with `noUncheckedIndexedAccess: true`, where `items[0]!`, `items[items.length - 1]!` and `bytes[0] as number` all pass without a single error, while the same file's guard-style code stays honest. So the day the flag is turned on, the audit's own verification will report the codebase as clean at exactly the three places where the array-bounds reasoning was never actually done. In useFocusTrap the reasoning happens to hold (line 45 returns early on `items.length === 0`), but the guard is three lines away from the assertion and nothing links them; in base64.ts:17 the loop bound makes it hold too. The inconsistency is the tell: the same repo already prefers real guards for the same hazard at src/app/AppShell.tsx:70-71 (`const randomBook = targetPool[...]; if (!randomBook) return;`) and coalescing at src/lib/goodreads.ts:82 and :96 (`(table[0] ?? [])`, `(cells[index] ?? '')`). The 10 further `!` in test files (migrate.test.ts:93/103/113/116, toastStore.test.ts:25/25/30, reviewQueue.test.tsx:95/112, ProfileContext.test.tsx:16) are the same shape and would behave the same way.
findings.suggestedPatch: Delete the three assertions now, while they are provably no-ops — `const first = items[0];`, `const last = items[items.length - 1];`, `String.fromCharCode(bytes[i])` — all three compile unchanged under the current flags. This costs nothing today and buys a truthful signal later: when `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` is eventually enabled, these sites will then correctly fail and can be fixed with the guard pattern the repo already uses (`const first = items[0]; if (!first) return;`) rather than being silently waved through. Sequence it before, not after, any `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` adoption — enabling the flag first and only then removing the assertions inverts the safety. The 10 test-file `!` can be left until the flag lands; they are lower-stakes and are all guarded by preceding `toHaveLength` / seeding assertions.

findings.title: `AiError.cause` is a permanent `unknown` with zero readers — captured at every failure, never narrowed, never surfaced
findings.description: `AiError` declares `readonly cause?: unknown` as a parameter property, and `toAiError` faithfully populates it on line 63 with the original error from the Gemini SDK or from fetch. Nothing in the repo ever reads it: a grep for `.cause` across all 86 source files returns zero hits, in production code and in tests alike. This is the textbook 'unknown that became permanent' — a safer-than-`any` placeholder that never got narrowed because it never got consumed, so it now costs the ceremony of `unknown` and delivers none of the safety benefit. It also quietly shadows the ES2022 `Error.cause` that `AiError` inherits, while `super(message)` never forwards it, so `err.cause` reaching a devtools console or a future structured logger is populated by the subclass field rather than by the standard mechanism — an inconsistency nobody can currently notice because there are no readers. Severity is low because there is no runtime hazard; the cost is that the original SDK error is captured and then unreachable, and that the field's type gives a future reader no information about what it might hold.
findings.suggestedPatch: Pick one and commit to it. (a) If the cause is wanted for diagnosis, stop declaring a shadow field and use the standard channel — drop the parameter property and call `super(message, { cause })`, which inherits `Error.cause` and is what devtools, `console.error` and any future logger already understand; then narrow at the single point of use with `error.cause instanceof Error ? error.cause.message : String(error.cause)`. (b) If it is genuinely unused, delete the parameter and the argument at line 63. Do not leave it as `unknown` with no readers — that is the exact state the spec calls out as 'same as any plus extra ceremony'. Option (a) is preferable given `toAiError` collapses eight distinct SDK failure modes into one of eight canned strings; the original message is the only way to tell them apart when a user reports 'Something went wrong talking to Gemini'.
